title: 3.4.16 Lab: Rewrite 3 Named Functions as Arrows
description: Convert three function declarations into one-line arrow expressions and confirm each still behaves the same. Auto-graded.

steps.title: Write the three declarations
steps.instructions: Define three separate function declarations, each with a different job: for example one that returns a number, one that returns a true/false answer, and one that returns a string. Use the function name() {} form.

steps.title: Convert each to an arrow
steps.instructions: Rewrite each declaration as a const assigned a one-line arrow function, using implicit return. Keep the same parameters and the same returned value as the declaration it replaces. Give each arrow a new name; reusing a declaration's name in the same file is a SyntaxError.

steps.title: Call all three and log results
steps.instructions: Call each of the three arrows with sample arguments and log the results with console.log. Check each result is what the original declaration would have returned.

requirements.title: Three arrow functions
requirements.description: At least three const variables are assigned arrow functions. Help: 3.4.8 (The Shorthand Rules)
requirements.hint: Each arrow is a const with a name, an equals sign, its parameters, =>, then the body. You need three of them.

requirements.title: Implicit return used
requirements.description: Every arrow body is a bare expression: no arrow body starts with a brace. Help: 3.4.8 (The Shorthand Rules)
requirements.hint: Drop the braces and the word return. The one expression after => is returned for you.

requirements.title: console.log present
requirements.description: Code calls console.log. Help: 3.4.8 (The Shorthand Rules)
requirements.hint: Print with console.log so you can see the result and check it against what you expected.

requirements.title: Three named arrows, each called
requirements.description: Three different const names each hold an arrow with at least one parameter, and each one is called. Help: 3.4.8 (The Shorthand Rules)
requirements.hint: Give each arrow its own const name and at least one parameter, then call each one by its name: console.log(triple(4)).

requirements.title: Three function declarations
requirements.description: The three function declarations from step 1 are still in the file, beside the arrows that rewrite them. Help: 3.4.7 (The Same Function Three Ways)
requirements.hint: Keep the three declarations you wrote in step 1 (function name(...) { ... }) and write each arrow under its own new name.

requirements.title: all three results are printed
requirements.description: At least three values are printed. Help: 3.4.8 (Shorthand Rules)
requirements.hint: Call each of the three arrows and print every result. Printing the three results on one line, separated by commas, is fine.

checks.fail: Print the result of each of your three arrows (one console.log each, or all three in one).

aiCheck.rubricTitle: What the AI read in your code
aiCheck.prompt: The student wrote JavaScript for the lab "3.4.16 Lab: Rewrite 3 Named Functions as Arrows". The task they were given: Define three separate function declarations, each with a different job: for example one that returns a number, one that returns a true/false answer, and one that returns a string. Use the function name() {} form. You cannot run their code: read it and judge what it WOULD do. Judge each criterion by whether the idea is achieved, however the student wrote it. Different variable and function names, template strings, arrow functions, semicolons, spacing, quotes and order are all fine. Do not require any particular structure unless the criterion names one. Mark a criterion missing only when the idea is absent or the code does the opposite. Code inside a comment never runs. Write each note for THIS student's own code: in a not-met note, name the exact line or name in their code that causes the problem (quote at most a few words of it), say in plain words what it does now versus what the criterion needs, and give one concrete next thing to try, but do NOT write the corrected code. In a met note, say in one short phrase what in their code satisfied it. Do not use generic praise.
